fields.meaning: On the occasion of…
examples: With my marriage as the occasion, I started saving seriously.
Taking the defect incident as an opportunity, we strengthened our quality control system.
I want to use my transfer as a chance to take on a new field.
Let's take this opportunity to tidy up the room.
The major earthquake raised awareness of disaster prevention.
fields.explain:
Usually placed at the beginning of the sentence to introduce the reason for a change.
Goes well with verbs such as:見直す・切り替える・導入する・開始する・改定する.
Semi-formal style; suits company documents and announcements, but can also be used in everyday life.

• Takes the occasion/turning point N to start something new or to change a policy or lifestyle.
• Expresses an active, deliberate intention; usually has a positive/improving character.
• Can be used with a negative event if what follows is a corrective or reform measure.
fields.notes:
• Using “これを機に” in a work email tactfully suggests a change without being too pushy.
• Do not overuse it for trivial matters; the nuance of “機” should be reserved for significant changes.
mistakes: Used before a verb clause: incorrect; it needs an event noun.
Expressing a natural, unintended consequence: consider ～ため／～結果 instead.
Confused with ～をきっかけに: exams often test the nuance of formality and scale.

rows: Turning point, taking the occasion to change
<ruby>出産<rt>しゅっさん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>機<rt>き</rt></ruby>に<ruby>在宅<rt>ざいたく</rt></ruby><ruby>勤務<rt>きんむ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>切替<rt>きりかえ</rt></ruby>。

<ruby>友人<rt>ゆうじん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>助言<rt>じょげん</rt></ruby>をきっかけに<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>。

Neutral, less emphasis on a turning point
<ruby>来日<rt>らいにち</rt></ruby>の<ruby>機会<rt>きかい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>観光<rt>かんこう</rt></ruby>。

fields.meaning: Starting with…
examples: Starting with the Osaka performance, the nationwide tour will get underway.
Starting with the Kansai area, we will begin offering the new service.
Starting with this award, requests poured in one after another.
Kicking off with the spring campaign, various events will be held throughout the year.
Starting with the press conference, the topic spread across social media.
fields.explain:
Moderately formal; suits planning documents and news.
The input should be an event/place noun that can serve as a “starting point”.
What follows should express continuation/spread; avoid describing a single, isolated action.

• States the opening point of a series of similar events/activities that follow.
• Emphasizes planning/spread across space or time.
• Often used in the context of organizations, products, performing arts and community campaigns.
fields.notes:
• Effective in résumés/PR: 「海外展開を皮切りに、売上が拡大」.
• In event news, combine with round/phase markers: 第1弾、第1期.
mistakes: Attached to a one-off action with no continuation: unnatural.
Confusing “kickoff” with “turning point”: exams like to trick you between 皮切り and 機.
Used before a noun that is not an event/place (e.g. 能力、気持ち): does not fit.

rows: <ruby>名古屋<rt>なごや</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皮切<rt>かわき</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>展開<rt>てんかい</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>札幌<rt>さっぽろ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皮切<rt>かわき</rt></ruby>りにして<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>。
No emphasis on a time sequence; emphasizes inclusion
<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めとして<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>名所<rt>めいしょ</rt></ruby>。
More casual; also used for individuals
<ruby>読書<rt>どくしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>手始<rt>てはじ</rt></ruby>めに<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>び<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す。

fields.meaning: With… as the start
examples: Starting in Sapporo, a traveling exhibition will be held across the country.
Starting with this lecture, we will hold a series of seminars once a month.
Starting with the broadcast of the drama, tie-ins with related products were announced one after another.
Starting with the opening of a new store, we will accelerate our expansion into the Tohoku region.
Starting in Okinawa, a simultaneous nationwide cleanup campaign will be launched.
fields.explain:
Formal; preferred in planning documents, proposals and announcements.
Placed at the end of an adverbial clause, linking smoothly to the main predicate.
What follows must express continuation/expansion; avoid ending abruptly.

• Equivalent to ～を皮切りに: “starting with N as the kickoff”, followed by a series of similar activities.
• “して” makes its adverbial role toward the main predicate clear; often used in official documents, plans and announcements.
• Suitable when followed by verbs of step-by-step rollout: 開始する・展開する・導入する・実施する...
fields.notes:
• The “して” form helps long, multi-clause sentences keep a coherent rhythm in administrative writing.
• Goes well with expressions of frequency/roadmap: 順次・段階的に・第一弾・第1期など.
mistakes: Used when no series follows: unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with ～を機に: exams often test “series” vs “turning point”.
Input is not a clear event/place noun: error-prone.

rows: <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皮切<rt>かわき</rt></ruby>りにツアー。
When a formal rhythm and a clear link to the predicate are needed
<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皮切<rt>かわき</rt></ruby>りにして<ruby>展開<rt>てんかい</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>整理<rt>せいり</rt></ruby><ruby>整頓<rt>せいとん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>手始<rt>てはじ</rt></ruby>めに<ruby>改善<rt>かいぜん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>に<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まり<ruby>秋<rt>あき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わる。

fields.meaning: On the premise that…
fields.connection: N + (の) + 前提で / V plain form + 前提で
examples: We draw up the budget on the premise that staff will be increased next term.
We are proceeding with preparations on the assumption that the tournament will be held as scheduled.
It was designed on the premise of using the existing system.
Let's continue the discussion on the premise that you will stay in Japan long-term.
The contract was drawn up on the assumption that everyone would agree.
fields.explain:
Used when establishing a prerequisite for a plan/design/process.
Suits business, legal and technical writing; also natural in conversation when discussing plans.
Often used with:進める,設計する,作成する,組む,試算する,想定する,検討する.

• “On the premise/assumption that …”, then the action/design/plan that follows is carried out.
• The premise is treated as a necessary condition; if the premise changes, what follows may no longer be valid.
• Nuance of planning, business, legal matters and research; more formal than つもりで (subjective intention).
fields.notes:
• “前提” is a foundational condition; in technical documents it often appears as “前提条件”.
• “～前提での + N” is used, but “～を前提とした + N” is more formal/better.
• If the premise is uncertain, consider “想定で/想定のもとで” to loosen the constraint.
mistakes: Incorrect with a noun: × 安全を前提で → ◯ 安全を前提に/として.
Confused with つもりで (intention) → ～前提で is a “mandatory condition”, not just an intention.
JLPT often tests substitution: ～前提で vs ～としたら vs ～場合は; note the “applied by default” character of ～前提で.

rows: Used with a clause; planning nuance

N を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>に／として

<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>に
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すつもりで<ruby>片付<rt>かたづ</rt></ruby>ける

fields.meaning: Extremely…
examples: That remark in a public place is extremely rude.
For an amateur to attempt to reach the summit alone is extremely dangerous.
This procedure is extremely inconvenient, so it should be reviewed as soon as possible.
The result was utterly regrettable.
His shamelessness is utterly lacking in common sense.
It is a joy beyond compare; I am happy beyond words.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a strong subjective judgment, often to reproach/criticize.
Stiff, formal style; in conversation it is usually replaced by ほんとうに／とても／めっちゃ…
Can come before a noun to highlight its bad quality:失礼極まりない態度.

- Meaning: “extremely/to the utmost”, emphasizing a strong emotional judgment (usually negative: rude, dangerous, foolish…).
• Formal, written-language nuance; stronger than とても/非常に, close to “excessively/unacceptably”.
• Often used with fixed word sets: 失礼／不便／危険／不快／残念／愚か＋極まりない.
• Can also be used with positive words (嬉しいこと極まりない), but this is rare and literary.
fields.notes:
• Reading: 極まりない（きわまりない）.
• Natural collocations: 失礼／危険／不便／不快／無責任／不謹慎／愚か＋極まりない.
• For even greater formality, you can switch to ～の極み／遺憾の意など.
mistakes: Using it with a neutral adjective sounds forced (× 綺麗極まりない). Choose words with a strong/evaluative nuance.
Confused with 極めて（adverb） in vocabulary questions; pay attention to the grammatical function.
Dropping “こと” with an i-adjective: × 嬉しい極まりない → should be: 嬉しいこと極まりない.
Wrong nuance: 極まりない usually carries reproach; using it in the wrong context sounds rude.

rows: この<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>ない<ruby>幸<rt>しあわ</rt></ruby>せ
Neutral adverb; no strong judgmental nuance
<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ
Close in meaning but leans toward describing a state that has reached the extreme; <ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない emphasizes judgment
<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby><ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まる<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>

fields.meaning: To the extreme…
examples: That attitude in a public place is utterly lacking in common sense.
Saying something like that is extremely rude.
The financial plan is far too careless; it is an extremely dangerous investment.
His ideas are foolish beyond words.
This response is extremely unpleasant.
fields.explain:
Do not add an adverb of degree (とても、極めて) before極まる.
Mainly used with na-adjectives and nouns describing qualities; i-adjectives usually switch to another form (極めて + Adj).
A strong judgment that can sound harsh; consider the social context.

- Indicates the utmost degree of a quality (usually negative): “extremely/… to the extreme”.
- Used when the speaker makes a strong judgment; common in written language and commentary.
- Goes well with Sino-Japanese words carrying an evaluative nuance: 失礼, 無礼, 非常識, 危険, 愚劣, 不便, 不快...
fields.notes:
• Many fixed collocations; using it otherwise sounds forced: 失礼極まる/極まりない, 危険極まりない, 非常識極まる.
• Reading: きわまる. Distinguish it from きわめる (transitive verb).
• In newspaper headlines/court rulings: often used to add weight to a judgment.
mistakes: Used with an i-adjective: (x) 速い極まる → (o) 極めて速い / 迅速の極み.
Adding an adverb of degree before 極まる is redundant: (x) とても失礼極まる.
Wrong nuance: 極まる/極まりない are usually negative; の極み can be positive.

rows: <ruby>危険<rt>きけん</rt></ruby><ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない
Used with N; also has a positive meaning
<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>不適切<rt>ふてきせつ</rt></ruby>

fields.meaning: Not enough…
examples: The explanation was insufficient, so a misunderstanding arose.
To succeed, you still don't practice enough.
That criticism is not worth considering.
He was judged not worthy of trust.
Rumors like that are not worth worrying about.
fields.explain:
Use が to mark what is lacking; use は for contrast/topic.
～にはNが足りない states the criterion/goal clearly; a standard expression in reports/evaluations.
～に足りない is judgmental; often used with Sino-Japanese nouns.

- Basic meaning: lacking, not enough (time, money, people, ability...).
- The structure “～に足りない”: an evaluation that something is not worth doing (検討・信頼・議論...).
- Nuance: “Nが足りない” is neutral; “Nに足りない” is formal and critical.
fields.notes:
• “頭が足りない” disparages someone's intelligence; be careful with the context.
• “足りない” vs “足らない”: a difference in style; the meaning is the same.
• “取るに足りない” is a common set phrase, equivalent to 些細だ/大したことはない.
mistakes: Confusing “Nが足りない” (lacking in quantity) with “Nに足りない” (not worth it).
Using verbs arbitrarily with “～に足りない”: prefer standard collocations (検討・信頼・注目...).
Wrong particle: (x) 合格するに点数が足りない → (o) 合格するには点数が足りない.

rows: <ruby>人手<rt>ひとで</rt></ruby>が<ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>する

fields.meaning: Worthy of…
examples: This survey has secured a sample size sufficient for discussion.
He is a partner worthy of trust.
The latest report has content worth referring to.
That phenomenon can be said to be worthy of attention.
This situation gives sufficient cause for concern.
fields.explain:
The most natural combinations:信頼・信用・検討・議論・注目・参考・称賛・懸念/危惧+ に足る.
Usually comes before a noun to make clear the worthiness of that N.
Not used to mean “enough in quantity” (use足りる).

- Confirms that the target has enough value/standing for an evaluative act (trust, consideration, attention...).
- Usually attaches to Sino-Japanese abstract nouns; formal, rational nuance.
- Widely used in research reports, business documents and specialist media.
fields.notes:
• V-るに足る is used selectively; prefer verbs that nominalize naturally (信用する・懸念する・危惧する).
• In academic titles, “～に足る証拠/根拠” is a very common phrase.
• The potential form 足りる also appears as a modifier: 信頼に足りるN（equivalent to に足る in many contexts）.
Not to be lumped together with ～たる～ (): a different point.
mistakes: Used for quantity: (x) お金に足る → (o) お金が足りる.
Wrong collocation: (x) 楽しいに足る → use 価値がある/面白い instead of ～に足る.
Confusing the direction of evaluation: ～に足る (positive) ↔ ～に足りない (negative).

fields.meaning: All, every single… (ことごとく)
examples: His predictions were wrong every single time.
Every one of the proposals was rejected.
The typhoon ruined every last crop in the fields.

fields.meaning: Dare to…, venture to…, deliberately… (敢えて)
examples: Even though he knew it was dangerous, he dared to take on the challenge.
Knowing full well that I will meet opposition, I will venture to speak.
I decided to deliberately not touch on the minor details.

fields.meaning: Sure enough, just as expected (案の定)
examples: Sure enough, he showed up late.
I had a bad feeling, and sure enough, it started to rain.
Just as I expected, the shop was crowded.

fields.meaning: In advance, beforehand… (あらかじめ)
examples: Please make a reservation in advance.
Please send your questions by email beforehand.
If you prepare in advance, you won't have to panic.

fields.meaning: Precisely because… (emphasizing a reason: ばこそ)
examples: It is precisely because I care about you that I speak so strictly.
It is precisely because you are healthy that you can enjoy your work too.
It was precisely because I loved them that I chose to part.

fields.meaning: Must not…, it is forbidden to… (written language: べからず/べからざる+N)
examples: It says, "Keep off the grass."
No fishing here.
He is an indispensable figure in the political world.

fields.meaning: …was inevitable, naturally bound to lead to… (べくして)
fields.connection: Vる + べくして + Vた (repeating the same verb)
examples: This accident was bound to happen.
They were probably destined to meet.
The team with real ability won, as it was bound to.

fields.meaning: Manner of…, way of…; after (a period of time): for the first time in… (ぶり)
examples: His confidence came across in the way he spoke.
Returning home for the first time in five years, I was surprised at how the town had changed.
The way she works is impressive.

fields.meaning: Even… (not)… (だに/だにしない)
examples: Just imagining that it could end like that is frightening.
I never even dreamed that he was the culprit.
He did not move a muscle at what I said.

fields.meaning: Would have…, and yet (だろうに)
fields.connection: [sentence/clause] V plain form + だろうに
examples: If you had taken the medicine, you would have gotten better right away.
He must be having a hard time too, yet he keeps smiling.
It would have been fine if you had just consulted me.

fields.meaning: Whatever… may be (であれ/であろうと)
examples: Whatever the reason, violence is not acceptable.
No matter who the other person is, I won't change my attitude.
Whether child or adult, everyone should follow the rules.

fields.meaning: Both… and… (でもあり～でもある)
examples: He is both a doctor and a writer.
This job is both tough and enjoyable.
She is both my teacher and my friend.

fields.meaning: Not… at all, not in the least… (でも何でもない)
examples: This is no secret at all.
That is no coincidence whatsoever.
Injections? They don't hurt one bit.

fields.meaning: Isn't it the case that…? (ではあるまいか)
fields.connection: V plain form + の + ではあるまいか / N + (なの) / Na + (なの) / Aい + の
examples: Might he not be hiding something?
Isn't this method the safest?
Might the economy not get even worse?

fields.meaning: Cannot… no matter what (どうにも～ない)
examples: I just can't stand this heat.
It's a problem that can't be dealt with alone.
I'm so sleepy that I just can't get any work done.

fields.meaning: Smacking of…, sounding like… (恩着せがましい)
examples: I'd like you to stop talking as if I owe you a favor.
I don't want to say anything that sounds like an excuse.
Kindness that is forced on people is actually a nuisance.

fields.meaning: End up in the position of…, be forced into… (羽目になる)
examples: I missed the last train and ended up having to walk home.
I took the job on too lightly and ended up having to do it all by myself.
I played around too much and ended up having to study all night.

fields.meaning: Not worth…, not serious enough to… (ほどのことではない)
examples: It's just a scratch, so it's not serious enough to go to the hospital.
It's not worth going out of the way to report.
It's nothing to cry about.

fields.meaning: Would rather… (ほうがましだ)
fields.connection: V plain form + ほうがましだ / N + の
examples: If I have to work at a company like that, I'd rather quit.
It's better to keep quiet than to tell a lie.
If the food is like this, a convenience-store bento would be better.

fields.meaning: …as much as you like, …freely (食べ放題)
examples: This restaurant is all-you-can-eat for 90 minutes.
For 1,000 yen a month, you can watch unlimited movies.
The grass in the garden has been left to grow wild.

fields.meaning: Depending on… (いかんだ/いかんによっては)
examples: Whether you succeed depends on your effort.
Depending on the test results, hospitalization may be necessary.
Depending on the weather, the game may be postponed.

fields.meaning: Any…, whatever… (いかなる)
examples: In any situation, you must not lose your composure.
I intend not to give in to any hardship.
Whatever the reason, being late will not be accepted.
